nameStory: The "American starburst" name captures this lichen's dramatic radiating growth pattern that spreads outward like fireworks frozen in time. Unlike its cousin the Salted Starburst Lichen, this species is native to North America, earning it the "American" designation.
description: American Starburst Lichen is a leaf-like (foliose) lichen that forms distinctive circular patches on tree bark. It spreads outward in radiating lobes that create a starburst or rosette pattern, typically reaching 2-4 inches across. The surface appears grayish-green when dry and becomes more vibrant green when wet. This bark-dwelling lichen belongs to the shield lichen family, one of the most common lichen groups in New England.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms circular rosettes with lobes radiating outward from the center like spokes of a wheel, creating an unmistakable starburst pattern when viewed from above

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green to pale green when dry, becoming noticeably more vibrant and saturated green when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows directly on tree bark, never on rocks or soil, with a preference for hardwood trees like oak and maple

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels thin and papery when dry, with smooth upper surface and distinct radiating ridges that you can trace with your finger

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual rosettes typically measure 2-4 inches across, though older specimens can grow larger and occasionally merge with neighboring patches

habitat: Look for American Starburst Lichen on the bark of deciduous trees throughout New England's forests, particularly on oak, maple, and birch trees. It prefers moderately shaded areas in mixed hardwood forests and can be found from sea level to mid-elevation mountains. You'll often spot it on the main trunks and larger branches of mature trees.

seasonality.spring: Becomes vibrant green during spring rains, making it easier to spot against darker bark. The radiating pattern is most obvious when the lichen is wet and expanded.
seasonality.summer: Appears more grayish and contracted during dry spells, but still maintains its distinctive starburst shape. Look for it in shadier spots where it stays slightly more hydrated.
seasonality.fall: Often most noticeable in fall when deciduous leaves drop, revealing lichen-covered bark more clearly. The rosette pattern stands out well against bare branches.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible year-round but appears muted and grayish. Snow and ice can highlight the circular growth pattern by outlining the edges of each rosette.

funFact: This lichen can essentially pause its life for months at a time - when completely dry, it goes dormant and can survive extreme conditions, then instantly "wake up" and resume growing within minutes of getting wet, like a biological on-off switch.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other circular foliose lichens, but the distinctive radiating starburst pattern with well-defined lobes sets it apart from the more irregular, ruffled edges of common shield lichens. Remember: if it looks like a perfect green firework frozen on bark, it's likely your starburst lichen.
compareHints: American Starburst Lichen differs from its close relative, Salted Starburst Lichen, primarily in its range and subtle chemical differences that require laboratory testing to distinguish. In the field, both species look nearly identical with their characteristic radiating rosette pattern. Other shield lichens in the same family typically have more irregular, less organized growth patterns without the neat spoke-like arrangement.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The key difference from its cousin American Starburst Lichen is the reproductive strategy - Salted Starburst reproduces with white powdery soredia while American Starburst uses small coral-like projections called isidia.
